content: 1. Pregnant women with Lassa fever have shown clinical improvement following spontaneous abortion or delivery. Uterine evacuation in these patients appears to reduce maternal mortality. However, obstetrical procedures must be performed with extreme caution due to the risk of nosocomial transmission and the potential for maternal hemorrhage, similar to the precautions taken in Ebola cases. 2. Breastfeeding women infected with Ebola, Marburg, Lassa fever, or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) may have already transmitted the virus to their breastfeeding infants through breast milk or close physical contact. Ebola and Marburg viruses have been detected in breast milk, and during the 2005 Marburg outbreak in Angola, breastfeeding was implicated in virus transmission. 3. There is limited data on managing breastfeeding in mother-infant pairs where one or both are infected. Current recommendations are based on anecdotal cases and limited field experience, assuming that the presence of Ebola virus in breast milk increases the risk of severe disease in already-infected infants. 4. Safe and sustainable feeding with appropriate breast milk substitutes (BMS) is necessary for newborns and some infants. Ready-to-use infant formula (RUIF) is preferred over powdered infant formula (PIF) due to reduced preparation risks. However, both RUIF and PIF can promote bacterial growth, necessitating strict hygiene of feeding utensils and adequate supplies for at least six months. 5. Breastfeeding should be suspended if RUIF is available and acceptable until breast milk tests negative for the virus. If artificial feeding is not possible, breastfeeding may continue with complementary foods for infants aged 6–23 months. Mothers and infants should be separated in treatment units when artificial feeding is feasible. 6. Lactating women who test positive for Ebola and have a negative or asymptomatic infant should suspend breastfeeding and use RUIF or expressed breast milk if possible. The infant should be cared for in an observational unit by a survivor caregiver and monitored as a contact. 7. Lactating women discharged as cured (after two consecutive negative blood PCR tests) should not resume breastfeeding until two negative breast milk PCR tests are obtained. Breast milk from women who had acute Ebola during pregnancy should be tested for the virus, and breastfeeding should be suspended if viral RNA is detected. 8. Wet nursing is not recommended due to the high risk of virus transmission between the wet nurse and the infant. 9. Infants and young children of acutely ill or Ebola-positive mothers are at high risk of infection. Infants recently breastfed by Ebola survivor mothers with positive breast milk should also be considered high risk. 10. Psychosocial support is crucial for mothers separated from their infants. Mothers who abruptly stop breastfeeding need assistance to express breast milk to alleviate pain, prevent engorgement, and avoid inflammation, especially within the first month postpartum. 11. Nutritional support is essential for all Ebola-infected patients, as the disease severely impacts nutritional status and immune response. Symptoms such as poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea impair food consumption and nutrient absorption. Nutritional care should balance the patient’s needs with their ability to tolerate food. 12. Nutritional support for Ebola patients includes three feeding phases: maintenance feeding, transition feeding, and boost feeding, alongside an initial rehydration phase if necessary. Food should be easily digestible during the maintenance phase, with a focus on nutrient-rich diets during recovery. 13. Patients unable to eat should be hydrated with oral rehydration solutions (ORS) or intravenous fluids if severely dehydrated. Nutritional support should be introduced gradually to avoid overloading impaired body systems, particularly the liver. 14. Children under five years should have their nutritional status assessed using mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) tapes and checked for bilateral pitting edema indicative of kwashiorkor. Severely malnourished children should be treated according to national protocols, considering the principles of Ebola treatment. 15. Vitamin A supplementation should be provided to children under five who have not received it in the last six months, unless they show signs of deficiency or measles. Severely malnourished children should only receive high-dose vitamin A if fortified foods are unavailable. 16. Nutritional support should include the minimum recommended daily allowance of nutrients through traditional and fortified foods. Patients receiving adequate fortified ready-to-use food may not require additional multivitamins. 17. For infants under six months discharged from treatment units, adequate amounts of RUIF should be provided until they reach six months. Caregivers should receive nutrition education on the safe use of RUIF and complementary feeding. 18. Home visits within two weeks of discharge should be scheduled to assess the infant’s outcome, if feasible. Cases of orphans should be reported to child protection teams to ensure proper linkage to welfare and social services. 19. Monitoring of severely ill patients should include regular reassessment for emergency clinical signs, input and output monitoring, and bedside documentation. Staff should be trained to measure waste volumes accurately.
